Marie Antoinette is an Austrian princess, newly arrived in Versailles to become queen of France. As we sweep down into the streets, fusing 2D and CG 3D, Antoinette surveys the scene that she sees from her carriage. She spies one face that catches her interest. “France has such beautiful lords,” she comments to her aide. But the ‘lord’ in question, Oscar, is a lady.

Riyoko Ikeda’s 1972 manga The Rose of Versailles is legendary. A historical drama for young female readers, set in 18th-century France around the time of the Revolution, it follows the magnetized destinies of two women, and the suitors and challengers that orbit them. Ostensibly a heterosexual story, yet rich in subtext of impossible love and androgynous gender presentation, The Rose of Versailles paved the way for many other seminal shojo anime and manga series such as Revolutionary Girl Utena and Le Chevalier D’Eon.

In 2025, studio MAPPA produced a new anime feature adaptation of The Rose of Versailles, which was distributed by Toho Next and Avex Pictures, and later licensed by Netflix. The film surprised audiences by being a full-fledged musical, boasting fifteen vocal numbers in total. These tracks are accompanied by kaleidoscopic, gleefully melodramatic music video set pieces – moments akin to anime opening and ending animations, but multiplied.

The adaptation’s director, Ai Yoshimura, worked at Sunrise before launching a successful freelance career. Her other directorial credits include Ao Haru Ride and Dance with D. As her film screened at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival – celebrated in a retrospective screening as part of the Women Directors: Diverse Visions sub-strand – Yoshimura was kind enough to answer our questions about adapting a storied manga classic.

Cartoon Brew: How did you come to work on this project?

Ai Yoshimura: I had previously worked with the producer from Avex on another project. After that wrapped up, they asked me what kind of project I’d like to tackle next. That’s when I stepped forward and said, “I’d love to do The Rose of Versailles!”

Did you grow up reading the original manga? What makes The Rose of Versailles special to you?

I remember finding the manga on my older cousin’s bookshelf when I was a child and getting completely absorbed in it. Back then, I just loved the pretty dresses and how cool Oscar was. Reading it again as an adult changed my perspective. I found myself deeply captivated by French history and the human drama of the people living in that era.

The musical numbers are some of the film’s most elaborate and exhilarating sequences. They resemble the opening and closing sequences of a TV anime, but you get to do this over and over in a single film. How did you approach directing them?

Incorporating songs into the structure was part of the plan from the very beginning. In the context of the story, the songs emphasize certain moments. They signal to the audience, “Pay close attention here. This is an important moment.”

For the visuals, we took an approach much like an opening or closing sequence. Instead of building the visuals around characters singing, I felt there was much more creative freedom in editing shots together to prioritize the music and the emotional imagery of the scene. We also had to consider the cost of hand-drawn animation.

How did you combine 2D and CG animation in the film?

We incorporated 3D to really bring the world of The Rose of Versailles to life, adding depth to show the kinds of people living there and the richness of the scenery. In the scene right before the title card, we used dynamic camerawork to capture a bustling crowd at the Palace of Versailles, giving the audience a sweeping look at the entire world right from the start.

You stay close to the manga’s character designs, especially those large, sparkling eyes, and keep the characters’ faces relatively still. Did the expressiveness of the original designs let you keep facial movement to a minimum?

When it came to character design, we focused on staying as faithful to the original work as possible. Even the highlights in their eyes were meticulously crafted by Oka-san, our character designer, to capture that original look. There are definitely parts where the acting is a bit more subtle and the focus is on the intricate details of the hair and costumes. Since the character models themselves have a lot of visual presence and volume, I feel that the performances still come across as convincing even with limited movement.

The manga is celebrated for its playfulness with gender presentation and androgyny. Do you think manga and animation give you a particular freedom to explore the fluidity and ambiguity of gender?

Manga and animation are works of imagination, so there’s a real sense of freedom to them, and I think the boundless possibilities they offer are what make them so fascinating. In The Rose of Versailles, the story really captures how characters constrained by the gender norms of their time establish their own identities and make their own choices. I think that’s where the true sense of liberation comes from.

Did you draw any inspiration from anime influenced by the original manga, such as Revolutionary Girl Utena or Le Chevalier D’Eon?

I was only familiar with the title of that anime, so it didn’t particularly influence me this time. As a fan of the series myself, I definitely took inspiration from the original TV anime, the Takarazuka Revue stage productions, and the live-action film. Some of those influences are pretty niche, so it’s hard to tell you exactly where they are, but I really hope fans of each adaptation will spot them and enjoy finding those little touches.

What do you hope a new audience takes away from your version of The Rose of Versailles?

The Rose of Versailles has been loved in so many different forms in the 54 years since its serialization began. I’m truly happy and deeply moved that this theatrical anime adaptation has become a new chapter in that long history. Along with enjoying this film, I hope audiences will also explore the past adaptations and come to love the original manga even more. It would be an honor if people continued to hold The Rose of Versailles close to their hearts forever.

Laika’s Wildwood is the only fully animated feature among the 20 films still in contention for the visual effects Oscar at the 99th Academy Awards.

Variety broke the news, reporting that the Academy’s VFX Branch notified the teams behind the 20 films ahead of the upcoming holiday weekend. Unlike the animated feature list, revealed publicly earlier this week, the Academy keeps the longlist private and will announce a 10-film shortlist on December 15. Because we’re working from a non-official list, the studios that executed the VFX work on these films are not included. Hopefully, when the Academy releases its shortlist, those outfits will be credited.

Wildwood, also among the 38 films eligible for animated feature, represents Laika’s second effects nomination, following Knight’s Kubo and the Two Strings in 2017.

As we reported after visiting Laika’s Portland studio and attending effects supervisor Steve Emerson’s View Conference masterclass, the Wildwood VFX team, with help from Weta, scanned physical assets in high resolution, capturing their colors and textures to build digital set extensions. Wētā FX contributed to the film’s gargantuan 12-minute final battle sequence.

Disney has four films on this year’s list, including The Mandalorian and Grogu, Avengers: Doomsday, Whalefall, and the live-action Moana. Godzilla Minus Zero follows up its 2024 category-winning predecessor Godzilla Minus One, while both of Denis Villeneuve’s previous Dune films won the category, making his third entry in the franchise a strong contender for this year’s prize, and 2027 one of the hardest fields to predict in a long time.

The 10 shortlisted films will go on to the visual effects bake-off in January. The five nominees will be announced January 21, and the Oscars will take place March 14.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Melk, written and directed by Belgian filmmaker Filip Anthonissen and produced by Brecht Van Elslande for Animal Tank. His first professional film, it won the Pardino d’Oro for Best International Short Film at Locarno, where it also became the festival’s short film candidate for the European Film Awards. Set in a remote 19th-century village, it follows an elderly woman searching for her adult son after a drunken incident, before the apparent arrival of the devil sends events spiraling into chaos.

Drawing on his childhood on a farm, Anthonissen explores the destructive effects of expectations and the pressure to fit in. His CG approach incorporates motion capture and simulation techniques, while the visual design takes inspiration from the Flemish Primitives. After working primarily in video installations, he used Melk to explore more structured storytelling, balancing clarity with ambiguity as a small family incident grows into a tragedy of near-mythological proportions.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Filip Anthonissen: The concept for Melk stems from thinking about my own childhood, growing up on a farm in a small town. Being different wasn’t encouraged, and there were a lot of expectations to fit in with everyone else. This idea of expectations, how they are internalized, and how destructive they can end up being was something I really wanted to make a film about. At the same time, the story itself isn’t overly personal, which allowed me to still have fun with it.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

It was my first narrative short, so I learned a lot about dramatic structure and pacing. Before this short, I made mostly video installations, heavy on concept and visuals, but without a clear story. The scenes were slow and wide, with minimal editing. So Melk was a big change for me, as storytelling became central. I had to learn how to guide the audience enough for them to understand what’s happening, while still leaving enough room for interpretation and ambiguity.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I’ve been working with 3D animation for a long time, but more recently I dove deeper into character animation. Having a background in motion graphics, I still draw from those techniques, particularly for simulations. Part of the animation was done using motion capture, which echoes the film’s theme of performing and having to play a role to fit in.

Visually, I drew a lot of inspiration from the Flemish Primitives, because I wanted to ground the film in my own heritage.

The story begins with a relatively small mistake before spiraling into absolute chaos. How did you decide how far to push that escalation?

I knew from the start that I wanted to push the escalation to a dramatic climax. I was inspired by Greek epics, where the protagonist unknowingly brings about their own downfall, and where the tragedy is often inflicted on them through family ties. The challenge was figuring out how to get to that point while keeping the intentions and motivations of the characters clear.

At the box office, The Cat in the Hat reached $70 million worldwide, while Wildwood passed The Boxtrolls’ domestic total ahead of Hexed’s Thanksgiving weekend arrival.

Aardman’s 50th anniversary festivities will continue late into the year with a new BBC documentary that dives deep into the Bristol stop-motion studio’s archives. Cracking Job Gromit: Aardman at 50 will air on BBC One and stream on BBC iPlayer this Christmas. An exact broadcast date hasn’t been announced, and today’s release didn’t specify international distribution plans.

Directed by Yemi Bamiro and produced by Mitre Studios, the film includes previously unseen footage and newly made animation with early sketches, character designs, and development artwork. It looks back at the early Wallace & Gromit adventures and goes behind the scenes of one of the best-loved studios in the world.

According to Bamiro:

Aardman is a beloved British institution whose work has the special ability to speak to everyone. It’s been such a privilege to be a part of this project and to tell their story for this incredible milestone of 50 years. I hope the film is able to shine a light on the commitment, talent, and dedication that goes into making an Aardman film or TV series. I’ve been blown away by some of the things I’ve seen behind the scenes. The production staff and I have all felt like giddy little kids every day working on this film, getting to see behind the curtain and understand how the magic gets made. It’s a special process perfectly executed by a special company.

Among the fans and collaborators to be featured in the doc are Ben Whitehead, the current voice of Wallace, along with Rob Brydon, Thandiwe Newton, Lenny Henry, Romesh Ranganathan, Nick Mohammed, Amelia Dimoldenberg, Lauren Patel, and Jordan Stephens.

Aardman’s roots date back to 1976, when co-founders Peter Lord and David Sproxton moved to Bristol and began producing animation professionally there. One of their earliest creations was Morph, the clay character who made his television debut the following year on the BBC children’s art show Take Hart.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is To the Woods (Une fugue), directed by Agnès Patron, co-written with Johanna Krawczyk, and produced by Sacrebleu Productions. The dialogue-free French film premiered at Cannes Critics’ Week and won TIFF’s Best Animated Short Film Award in 2025 before earning its Oscar qualification through the Grand Prix at Anima Brussels in 2026.

Inspired by Patron’s grandmother, who lost her older brother as a child, the film explores the bond between siblings and the ways memory preserves and transforms those we lose. Patron painted the images by hand in gouache, blending the children into nocturnal landscapes that reflect their inner worlds. Small differences in movement, shifting backgrounds, and the selective absence of sound distinguish the sister’s physical presence from her brother’s increasingly elusive one.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Agnès Patron: My family memories were a genuine source of inspiration for this film. My grandmother, on whom the story is based, lost her older brother in a car accident when she was very young. She loved and admired him deeply, and this loss remained with her throughout her life.

I grew up with this story, and I also have a brother whom I love deeply. Today, I am the mother of a son and a daughter, so questions around family bonds, love, and loss have naturally become part of my own reflections.

Making this film was also a way of reconnecting with those I have lost. The film has become a kind of talisman for me.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

The fully developed images came together quite late in production, and I had to learn to embrace this gradual construction rather than seek immediate certainty. The animated tests created during pre-production became my compass, allowing me to stay connected to the film’s original intentions while the visual world was taking shape.

I also learned how much precision can be required to achieve simplicity. We worked closely with the team from the posing stage onward to reduce each movement to its essence. I became more aware of how much emotional intensity can emerge from the smallest gesture, and how essential it is to make every choice meaningful.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

Everything in the film is painted by hand. I love the relationship with the material itself, its texture, its vibrations, its pulse.

For this story, the night and the settings were essential. I wanted to create a sense of blur, an atmosphere that was rich but not overloaded with detail, where the characters and the landscape could almost become one.

I wanted the children to feel both present and fragile, as if they were emerging from the darkness. This is why I chose gouache, a technique that allows for very soft transitions and helps me blend the characters into their surroundings. It was a way of making the landscape an extension of their inner world.

How did you use movement and pacing to distinguish the warmth of childhood memories from the more unsettling moments in the film?

As a child, Sister is very lively. Her movements are more sudden, and she changes direction or mood very quickly. Brother is slower, more peaceful, and less expressive. His animation is more restrained because he is already a memory, something that is gradually fading away.

In the forest, when Sister loses Brother, we worked on the movement of the backgrounds, on blurring, and on the feeling of losing your bearings. I wanted the landscape itself to reflect Sister’s emotional turmoil.

As an adult, Sister has become heavier, carrying the grief of losing her brother. In these scenes, Brother no longer has any sound effects. I wanted to make his presence feel more ghostly, without relying on opacity effects.

In Disney’s Hexed, hitting theaters on Wednesday, November 25, an impulsive teenager named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) discovers she has magical abilities and winds up in Hexe, a hidden realm of witches, with her overly cautious mother, Alice (Rashida Jones). Along the way, they encounter the formidable Queen Celeste (Jodie Foster) and a three-eyed cat named Beef Roger (Walton Goggins), whose magic comes with a little sparkling cat litter.

Ahead of the film’s holiday release, directors Fawn Veerasunthorn (Wish) and Jason Hand (Moana 2) and producers Roy Conli and Yvett Merino sat down with us to discuss building a world where you can tell more about a person by how they cast a spell than by how they look or speak. For Conli, getting to make up those rules from scratch was part of the appeal.

“I love originals because you have such freedom,” says Conli. “Once you’ve established a world, once you’ve established your characters and you’ve fallen in love with them, you can tell any story.”

Thanks in part to a mandate from the top, that freedom extended equally to the film’s sense of humor and adventure. Veerasunthorn recalls a conversation with Disney Animation chief creative officer Jared Bush, who co-wrote the film with Dana Ledoux Miller. “He said, ‘We can get weird with this one, you guys. We can push it really far. We can be edgy. We can present the feeling of danger that can be thrilling.’” The film they made, she says, is “emotional, but it’s also wildly funny and janky and weird.”

“Magic for us is a metaphor for a person’s potential,” she explains. “It’s a visual representation of that. Therefore, each person’s magic must look different from one another.”

For most, if not all, of the film, Billie is only figuring out what she can and can’t do, and Veerasunthorn wanted her magic to reflect that lack of control. “Celeste already figured herself out, so her magic is elegant, has a tremendous sense of control,” she says. “Her magic is beautiful in a way that you’re leaning in and you’re being lured or tempted by it a little bit. Even Billie should feel that.”

Effects designers Dan Lund and Michelle Sharp took a similar character-first approach to Beef Roger’s spellcasting. “What if he has a bunch of cat hair that poofs out with it?” Hand recalls. “And it’s got a little bit of cat litter that sparkles, and then mix in a little fizzy drinkness to it that just made it so specific to him.”

Although the film is set today, Veerasunthorn says the team imagined the land of Hexe originating in the 1700s, when people could be accused of witchcraft for doing things others misunderstood. “What if there is a place where you can actually be free to explore all your potentials in the world,” she says, “a place that’s made by witches for witches?”

The filmmakers gave Hexe a Northeastern look and put it in a perpetual, Northeastern fall. Think Salem, Massachusetts postcards. “What if this is a place where the rain has just got done cleaning everything out, and the air is crisp, and there’s fall all the time?” says Veerasunthorn. “It’s like forever autumn as a city.”

“[Production designer] Lorelay talks about how she was inspired by the witch’s hats and the pointiness and triangles of it,” Merino says of Lorelay Bové, explaining the look and logic of Hexe’s architecture. “Our look team did an amazing job of actually hyper-focusing on the texture of it so it feels real to us, even though it’s a fantasy world.”

Character designers dug through Disney’s own library for examples of how far they could push proportions. Hand remembers putting the new designs side by side with characters from the Milt Kahl era and noticing details like the width of a wrist or particularly lanky limbs. “We realized we had a long way to go to get back to the caricature level that we used to do,” he says. The effort, the team argues, was well worth it in the end, and gave the animators room for physical comedy, particularly in scenes of flight and fancy.

Conli gives a great deal of the credit to character designer Bill Schwab, calling him “an absolutely brilliant designer who can go super, super caricatured and super real.” The actors informed the designs, too. “I remember when we cast Jodie, we actually updated Celeste’s design,” says Veerasunthorn. “This is Jodie Foster. This is her mannerism we study. Her facial expressions. I hope that’s not creepy, but that’s what we do.”

With a diverse realm to explore, the filmmakers made sure to keep the story tightly focused on Billie and Alice and their evolving relationship. “We only have to understand that Alice is doing everything to protect Billie from harm,” says Veerasunthorn. “All the other story beyond that is not something that we find essential to the heart of this film.”

Beef Roger, Alice’s familiar, gives Billie a glimpse of who her mother was before she became a parent. “It’s like us meeting our mom’s friend and that person’s a little weird,” says Veerasunthorn. “And then you’re like, ‘This doesn’t compute. How were you friends? There’s got to be more to the story.’”

Beef makes Billie curious about Alice’s life in Hexe, while Celeste gives her a sense of why she left it. For Conli, the most unsettling thing about the queen was a quality that needed no special effects. “I don’t think there’s anything spookier than a narcissist,” he says. “And that’s what Celeste is. It’s all about her.”

For Hand, the test was whether the world they’d built could sweep audiences up long enough for Billie and Alice’s story to catch them by surprise. “I think it’s that reason we all went to the movies in the first place,” he says, “to go and be swept away by a story that brings you to literally a different world in this movie, and for the emotional story to sneak up on you.”

Titmouse is developing an animated series based on Image Comics’ Fireborn, co-created by Curt Pires and Franklin Jonas, with artist Patrick Mulholland. Pires and Jonas will executive produce through Pires’ TECC Content and work directly with the super-indie studio behind The Legend of Vox Machina and Star Trek: Lower Decks.

In the comic, Aaron Hillburg, the unruly teenage son of a billionaire, has his life upended when he merges with a dragon egg. Suddenly bonded to an ancient mystical force, the character is pulled into a magical underworld beneath New York City. According to the companies, their animated adaptation will hold true to the published version’s distinct neon palette, ’90s comic-book excess, and 16-bit gaming influences, with grand aerial chases and fights capable of leveling skyscrapers.

In a release, Pires explained:

Fireborn is a kinetic, bombastic action series perfect for animation, and Titmouse is the perfect animation studio to collaborate with. From Scavenger’s Reign to Golden Axe, the studio’s dedication to storytelling and excellence is unrivaled. They’re bringing their breakneck, kinetic chaos to Fireborn. We’re excited to take Fireborn to new heights.

Jonas added:

I’m so so so stoked that Titmouse and all of us on the Fireborn team are embarking on this journey together. I’m such a huge fan of their studio’s entire catalogue and I’m over the moon excited to see what legendary fun we can cook up together.

And Titmouse creative director Alexei Shay said:

Fireborn embraces a crazy energy, and I’m here for it. Its creators clearly have reverence for the worldbuilding and the references they’re winking at, but they’re also not afraid to set all of that on fire at any given moment if that’s what will ultimately raise the stakes and make for the best story. And in the end, aren’t they right to burn this all down and replace it with something more exciting? Something bigger, stranger, more fantastical? Something new? I say yes, let’s do that. When can we start?

Fireborn launched in April as a spinoff of Pires’ Lost Fantasy. Its first issue sold out at the distributor level, so another edition was ordered to print. The first collected edition, which gathers issues one through four, is available now, as is the fifth issue, a crossover with Lost Fantasy. The release didn’t address distribution, and no broadcaster or streaming partner was announced.

The BBC has struck a deal to bring a raft of its top kids’ series, such as Hey Duggee, Numberblocks, and Teletubbies, to a dedicated CBeebies hub on Netflix as the U.K. public broadcaster looks for new ways to reach young viewers while cutting costs.

In total, 24 preschool shows will be available on the platform, which will launch in the U.K. on December 2.

The deal is an important one for the country’s original production landscape, as the BBC is the U.K.’s biggest commissioner of children’s programming but is looking to cut half a billion pounds in spending. Earlier this year, as part of those cuts, it announced plans to eliminate about 1,800 jobs and close some programs and services. Falling license fee income (in the U.K., households that watch live TV or use BBC iPlayer generally pay an annual license fee that helps fund the BBC) and rising production costs have squeezed its finances, while streaming, gaming, and YouTube compete for kids’ attention.

In addition to the catalog content, Netflix has committed to funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions. BBC Studios will also handle a deal to distribute CBeebies shows to Netflix subscribers outside the U.K., aiming to bring more investment into British children’s programming.

Some CBeebies favorites, like Shaun the Sheep, are already available on Netflix, but this will be the first time that the preschool brand will have its own bespoke space on the platform.

BBC chief content officer Kate Phillips said the trial is meant to help more viewers discover CBeebies, specifying that “this limited trial will make a curated selection of CBeebies programs available on Netflix, while BBC iPlayer remains the home of the full CBeebies experience.”

Anne Mensah, Netflix’s vice president of Netflix’s UK content, added: “We want to build a fun and safe space parents can feel good about, with content their kids will love.”

For the BBC, the experiment comes down to whether putting some of its best-known kids’ shows on a service families already use can bring in viewers it’s missing. For Netflix, it adds two dozen well-known preschool titles in one go.

A record 38 films are eligible for the Animated Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards, topping the previous record of 35 set last year.

This year’s lineup includes both of Pixar’s 2026 features, Hoppers and Toy Story 5, alongside Disney’s Hexed, Sony Pictures Animation’s GOAT, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s The Cat in the Hat, and Laika’s Wildwood. Netflix has the largest slate of any distributor, which includes Brad Bird’s Ray Gunn; the company’s first end-to-end in-house animated feature, Steps; Skyedance’s other 2026 title, Swapped; the French-Belgian pickup In Waves; and the Mexican stop-motion feature I Am Frankelda. Dave Green’s Coyote vs. Acme is also in the running after some early doubts about whether the live-action hybrid contained enough animation to qualify.

From outside the major U.S. studios, Leah Nelson’s Tangles and Louis Clichy’s Iron Boy both come out of Cannes, where the latter won a special jury prize in Un Certain Regard. Cartoon Saloon is once again in the mix with Louise Bagnall’s Julián, Aardman returns with Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom, and Canadian musician and graphic novelist Kid Koala makes his feature directing debut with Space Cadet.

Seven anime titles made this year’s list, from franchise entries like Mobile Suit Gundam Hathaway: The Sorcery of Nymph Circe to more idiosyncratic films like Jinsei and Grotesqqque. Masanao Kawajiri’s Cherry and Virgin and Kohei Kadowaki’s We Are Aliens, which played Cannes and Annecy before winning the top feature prize in Ottawa, feel like odd omissions here. Likely a distribution issue, the two were festival standouts this year, the latter screening in Cannes and winning the top prize at Ottawa. Chinese artist Sun Xun’s Magic Atlas is a similarly surprising miss on the list, having received an honorable mention in Ottawa and a special jury prize at the Tokyo International Film Festival earlier this month.

The Academy explained the current nomination rules in a release, writing:

To determine the five nominees, members of the Animation Branch are automatically eligible to vote in the category. Academy members outside of the Animation Branch are invited to opt in to participate and must meet a minimum viewing requirement to be eligible to vote in the category. Films submitted in the Animated Feature Film category may also qualify for Academy Awards in other categories, including Best Picture. Animated features that have been submitted in the International Feature Film category as their country’s official selection are also eligible in the category.

The five films that receive the most votes will be announced as nominees on January 21, 2027. The Oscars ceremony will take place on Sunday, March 14.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Haboolm Ksinaałgat (Soul Catcher), directed by Amanda Strong with co-director and screenwriter Pamela Post, and made independently through Spotted Fawn Productions. The Canadian film combines stop-motion puppets and physical sets with CG effects, executed across a five-year production. After its world premiere at TIFF, it qualified for Oscar consideration by winning the animation Grand Jury Award at the Edmonton International Film Festival.

Based on an incident from Post’s father’s childhood, the film follows a young Ts’msyen apprentice on a supernatural journey along the Ksyen, or Skeena River. An act of cruelty by a missionary becomes the starting point for a story of cultural reclamation and intergenerational healing. The filmmakers worked with First Nation artists to design the totem poles, creating digital models and hand-painted physical versions that could move between the production’s animation techniques.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Pamela Post: Soul Catcher is based on a true story from my Ts’msyen father’s childhood. He grew up in a tiny village on the Ksyen (Skeena River) in British Columbia. He was a much older dad. His stories were like time travel. I felt in my gut this was meant to be a stop-motion film and was an admirer of Amanda’s powerful work. The film depicts an act of cruelty against my dad and other Ts’msyen children by an old evangelical missionary in the early 20th century. It’s my way of righting that wrong through art.

Amanda Strong: My connection to the story started as a stop-motion mentor to Pamela. The power of Soul Catcher’s truths led to a deeper collaboration of co-direction. Indigenous stories are best told when made by Indigenous people. Our ancestors were calling through us to go on this five-year handmade journey together.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

Strong: Narrative sovereignty was integral for Pamela and me. We chose a harder path, producing independently without external production partners, which meant limited access to resources and financial support. Despite production challenges, we’re proud to own our film.

Stop motion is the slowest, most painstaking, and I think most soulful form of animation, especially precious in this era of AI, but it’s expensive and a lot of work. It’s a constant dance of trying to achieve the highest art with grant dollars that are getting harder to access. Having an amazing team of artists and cast bound to this story was essential to pushing through the creative and technical barriers.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

Strong: It was important for me to center this film in stop-motion techniques and physically built assets. To represent the vast landscapes, cultural objects, and VFX needs of the story, I knew we needed the aid of 3D. The technical process was a weaving of handmade and digital pieces. We had a lot of new creative challenges we hadn’t faced before. At its core, this hybrid process was the best approach to honoring the stop-motion art form while serving Pamela’s story and community.

Post: The film represents Ts’msyen culture, so centering the story, people, and land was key to its visual representation. From the old shaman’s bear-fur robe and bear-claw crown to the oolichan swimming among the eelgrass in the Skeena River, the monumental totem poles, and sacred rattles, the film is a kaleidoscope of our culture.

How did you approach bringing the century-old totem pole to life through stop motion, particularly given its spiritual and cultural significance?

Post: From a story perspective, my father’s words guided me. Because harm was done to a totem pole, and to my dad as a child, the injured totem pole became a metaphor for the harms of colonization. Returning it to its place of honor is a metaphor for cultural revitalization.

Strong: As a production studio, there are protocols we follow when making films with Indigenous stories and cultural belongings. Museums have a lot of totem poles in their collections, but they’re connected to families and have stories that can’t be copied. We collaborated with First Nation artists to design authentic poles in 2D, with a front and side view, and, with their guidance, modeled them in 3D, followed by 3D printing and hand-painting. Because we had both physical assets and 3D models, we realized we could use them interchangeably in our process.

ASIFA-Hollywood held its first Animation Showcase on November 14 and 15 at the Audrey Irmas Pavilion in Los Angeles. We were there, and I’d have published this article sooner, but Microsoft crashes, airspace shutdowns, a temporarily out-of-commission laptop, and jet lag all conspired to set me back a few days.

The showcase felt like a hit, even with some first-year growing pains. It was also a lot to pack into two days, and attending all or most of it would have probably felt like a marathon. Just ask ASIFA-Hollywood director Aubry Mintz or board member David Silverman, who powered through the full two days and looked ready for a few days off by Sunday evening.

An incredible lineup of speakers, exciting deep-dive presentations, and plenty of opportunities to meet filmmakers, artists, and producers from around the world kept the event moving. A typical FYC screening might give filmmakers a brief Q&A. Here, apart from a few short screenings, the Showcase gave presenters the stage for about an hour apiece. Across the weekend, that time went to behind-the-scenes footage, technical breakdowns, musical performances, and appearances by members of the voice casts.

Held as part of the Infinity Festival, the two-day event brought together filmmakers including Brad Bird (Ray Gunn), Travis Knight (Wildwood), Tyree Dillihay (GOAT), Leah Nelson (Tangles), Alyce Tzue and John Ripa (Steps), Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni (The Cat in the Hat), Joel Crawford and Januel P. Mercado (Forgotten Island), Daniel Chong (Hoppers), Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand (Hexed), Kenna Harris (Toy Story 5), and Louise Bagnall (Julián). And those are just the feature directors.

I also had the pleasure of moderating the weekend’s closing presentation, a conversation with Ervin Han and Raul Garcia, the directors of Annecy winner The Violinist, alongside the film’s composer, Ricky Ho.

The TV lineup included Bruce W. Smith (The Proud Family), David Silverman (The Simpsons), and Sean Gantka (X-Men ’97), while ASIFA-Hollywood board president Frank Gladstone moderated a panel on Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender with Lauren Montgomery.

The shorts got their fair share of stage time, too, with Pola Maneli and Rich Levy there for Apart, Nigel Tierney and Federico Heller for Addicted to It, and Josh Wassung for Optimus Prime: Awakening. Warner Bros. also gave a closer look at Daffy Season, its new Looney Tunes short from Hamish Grieve and Todd Wilderman that opened ahead of The Cat in the Hat at the box office in the last few weeks.

ASIFA-Hollywood reported more than 350 attendees and plans to bring the Showcase back in 2027. Giving artists room to get into the details of their work is what made the event stand out on a crowded awards-season calendar, and it’s what gives the Showcase room to grow. Mintz told us he’d like to record some of next year’s panels and possibly put them online. We’d love to see that happen.

Judging by this year’s presentations, the organizers know what they’ve got, and we’re excited to see what they do with it.

Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s The Cat in the Hat finished fourth at the North American box office over the Nov. 20–22 weekend, with the Dr. Seuss adaptation earning an estimated $6.9 million in its third frame, down 39%. That brings its domestic total to $47.1 million so far.

Directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja, the film was fifth worldwide with $10.6 million grossed, which included $3.7 million from international markets. To date, its total box office run sits at an estimated $70.2 million worldwide, including $23.1 million overseas. Surely that’s not good enough for a film that Variety says cost $92 million to make. The upcoming Thanksgiving weekend could inject some life back into the film’s domestic run, but it will compete against Disney’s big 2026 release, Hexed (more on that later), so hopes should stay tempered.

Laika’s Wildwood was still ticking along in its fifth weekend and overtook the $50.8 million domestic run of the studio’s 2014 feature The Boxtrolls on Saturday, when it earned $825,000 to reach $51.4 million. According to distributor Fathom Entertainment, Travis Knight’s stop-motion epic pulled in $2.1 million over the full weekend and now sits at $52.2 million domestically.

According to Box Office Mojo, Wildwood has now grossed $75.5 million worldwide, including $23.1 million from international markets. A few major releases are still on the horizon, with the film set to open in France on Dec. 9 and South Korea on Jan. 6.

Looking ahead, Walt Disney Animation Studios’ Hexed opens on Wednesday, ahead of Thanksgiving. Box Office Theory projects a $20 million to $29 million domestic opening from Friday through Sunday and $36.5 million over the five-day holiday. That would put Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand’s witch adventure ahead of Disney Animation’s last two original Thanksgiving releases, Wish, which opened to $31.6 million over five days in 2023, and Strange World, which bombed dramatically with only $18.9 million over the same stretch in 2022.

Seven South Korean animation studios went to Toronto earlier this month to pitch projects and meet North American buyers. The studios estimate those talks could lead to $50 million in business, from licensing and distribution to co-productions. Studio Shelter, the company behind the hit webtoon Maru Is a Puppy, took home the showcase’s top pitching prize for Brew & Banish Cafe.

The agreement comes at a timely moment for companies on both sides of the Pacific. Canada and South Korea signed an updated audiovisual co-production treaty in April, and the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA) said Canadian ratification was still pending at the time of the showcase. Once the treaty takes effect, qualifying projects can be treated as domestic productions in both countries. In practical terms, a Canadian producer could develop an animated series with a South Korean studio and still qualify for Canadian public funding and tax credits. That gives studios more options for putting together a budget while a project is still in development.

The K-Animation Global Showcase, held November 3–4, brought together representatives from 32 North American companies and organizations, including CBC Kids, TVOkids, Bell Media’s Crave, and U.S. distributor GKIDS. KOCCA, which hosted the event with South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, said the 112 one-on-one meetings covered everything from licensing and distribution to co-producing projects.

Participating studios put the potential value of the opportunities discussed at a hefty US $50 million.

At the showcase, Brew & Banish Cafe received the KOCCA President’s Award from a seven-member North American judging panel. Alexis McLaren, a production executive in original programming at Canadian streamer Crave and a member of the jury, said:

The project has familiar elements reminiscent of globally popular works, giving it the potential to capture viewers’ interest and resonate with them. The narrative’s fateful connection to the protagonist’s hidden past makes it exceptionally intriguing for international audiences.

Studio Shelter CEO Yang Jung-woo said the studio is already following up with buyers it met at the event:

We are thrilled that North American industry experts recognized both the creative quality and market potential of our story. We are actively advancing follow-up discussions with the buyers we met in Toronto as we launch into the North American market.

Don Bluth’s An American Tail opened in theaters on November 21, 1986. To mark its 40th anniversary, we’re revisiting some of the scariest moments in Bluth’s filmography.

If you’re familiar with Bluth’s movies, you know that each usually has at least one scene sure to terrorize children. We’ll start with the unforgettable thunderstorm in An American Tail, when the waves turn into monstrous sea gods.

https://t.co/aqtW48eSNQ

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

A lot of people talk about scenes from Disney movies that scared them as children. With a few exceptions, I don’t remember being particularly frightened by those. Sure, Ursula turning into a giant sea goddess in The Little Mermaid is hair-raising in the moment, but then she’s satisfyingly defeated and we all go away happily humming “Under the Sea.”

I distinctly remember being unsettled by several moments in Bluth’s movies as a kid, and I think it comes down to the sudden shifts in tone. Everything will be sugary sweet, and then out of nowhere the lighting turns harsh, the music gets ominous, and ravenous creatures are viciously attacking our heroes for reasons that are often hard to fathom.

Even in the more upsetting moments of a Disney or Pixar cartoon, you get the sense that the filmmakers have a firm grip on the story and will guide you to a happy ending. A Don Bluth picture can feel like a madman is at the wheel and you have no idea whether you’re about to ram into a lamppost. That’s part of what gives his movies their flavor, as this scene from An American Tail shows.

https://t.co/C9VxYYtyXe

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Bluth was a rising star at Disney in the 1970s. He animated on Robin Hood and The Rescuers, headed up the animation on Pete’s Dragon, and directed the short The Small One. In 1979, during production of The Fox and the Hound, Bluth decided Disney had lost its way. He staged a walkout, taking a team of artists with him to form Don Bluth Productions.

The studio’s first film, the short Banjo the Woodpile Cat (1979), began life in Bluth’s garage while he was still at Disney. The ferocious dogs give you a taste of the terrors to come, although the bouncy score, complete with xylophone, takes the edge off.

https://t.co/rZD5T7MV1S

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Bluth’s first feature, The Secret of NIMH (1982), is probably his best. I love its dark fantasy atmosphere, from the stellar painted backdrops and Jerry Goldsmith’s magical score to the lavish hand-drawn effects that look like something out of an early ’40s Disney feature. Bluth’s characters tend to gesticulate wildly, which makes Mrs. Brisby’s understated performance all the more striking. John Pomeroy’s animation of the menacing Great Owl is also outstanding.

https://t.co/ze1CWkBtki

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

The Secret of NIMH doesn’t shy away from unsettling imagery, especially when the scientists experiment on the rats. The psychedelic reaction to an injection is overwhelming, and the quiet that follows is just as unnerving.

https://t.co/3FHhWwVpuN

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Now regarded as a classic, The Secret of NIMH was trounced at the box office by E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial. Goldsmith introduced Bluth to E.T. director Steven Spielberg, who offered to produce Bluth’s next movie, telling him, “Make me something pretty like you did in NIMH.” It’s easy to see why Spielberg was impressed. The climactic sword fight is as exciting as it is brutal.

https://t.co/FE3zdbSZgR

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

With Spielberg on board, Bluth took on Disney with An American Tail (1986), about a family of mice who emigrate to the United States. It was a massive hit, outgrossing Disney’s The Great Mouse Detective that year.

As with NIMH, some moments are unusually dark for a family film. I remember being unnerved as a kid by the attack of the Cossack Cats, which takes place alongside a raid in which realistically drawn humans are attacked and killed. The scene draws on the pogroms that swept through southwestern Imperial Russia in the 1880s. Antisemitic propaganda blamed Jews for the 1881 assassination of Tsar Alexander II, and the ensuing violence helped spur mass emigration, including to the United States.

As he would later do with the Russian Revolution in Anastasia, Bluth uses real events as a backdrop and gives the audience little historical context. The violence can be especially jarring when you’re a kid going in cold.

https://t.co/dNHnNNNA1Z

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Production on An American Tail went smoothly, but Bluth’s follow-up, The Land Before Time (1988), hit some snags. Producers George Lucas and Steven Spielberg thought the T. rex was too scary, telling Bluth, “We’ll have kids crying in the lobby and a lot of angry parents. You don’t want that.” More than 10 minutes of footage were cut, much of it fully animated and in color. Most of it was lost. The cuts included a surprise attack by Sharptooth, close-ups of the dinosaur snapping its jaws, and an extended version of its fight with Littlefoot’s mother.

Bluth and Spielberg disagreed over the cuts and parted ways. Spielberg went on to direct a violent dinosaur movie of his own, Jurassic Park. Even after the cuts, Sharptooth still gets some great moments, like this one where Cera thinks the dinosaur is dead.

https://t.co/EiVtECHc7e

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Both Bluth-Spielberg collaborations have a sad, lonely mood. In each, a child is separated from their family and left in a cold, unfriendly world with something threatening around every corner. For a little kid, it’s just about the scariest thing imaginable. James Horner’s scores deepen that sense of loneliness.

https://t.co/IRAbLWP6ov

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Bluth’s bizarre supernatural fantasy All Dogs Go to Heaven (1989) also underwent last-minute changes. Several scenes were cut, and the Tommy guns were inexplicably replaced with ray guns. Charles B. Barkin’s dream of being sent to hell is a prime example of Bluth’s penchant for nightmarish imagery. Here’s the scene, along with a few moments deemed too creepy for the final cut.

https://t.co/99cE8O2uuV

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Rock-A-Doodle (1991), built around a rooster who spoofs Elvis Presley, has long fascinated me. The studio found the film confusing and disturbing, so it cut scenes and added nearly nonstop narration to explain what’s supposed to be happening. It also added lucky charms to the Grand Duke’s demonic breath and feathers to cover Goldie’s ample cleavage. Our hero even gets drunk on what looks like milk.

The changes made an already deranged movie even more deranged. The plot makes no sense, and every scene feels like a cutesy-poo kiddie movie, a zany cartoon comedy, and a terrifying horror fantasy all got tossed in a blender.

In this early scene, right after a musical number with a smiling sun, a character we’ve never met and will never see again savagely attacks our hero, Chanticleer. The narrator tries to explain by telling us he works for the villain, whom we also haven’t met yet. Then all of Chanticleer’s friends turn on him. I love this crazy movie, and I never get tired of trying to follow its dream logic.

https://t.co/WxH42NSTdI

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Bluth’s mid-’90s films, Thumbelina (1994), A Troll in Central Park (1994), and The Pebble and the Penguin (1995), were erratic and generally more lighthearted than his ’80s work. Still, Bluth rarely passed up a chance to draw a ferocious beast with gnashing teeth.

https://t.co/bDNQxQX4gQ

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Anastasia (1997) was Bluth’s comeback. With a bigger budget from 20th Century Fox, he delivered his first bona fide hit since the ’80s. The movie combines warped historical fiction with Disneyesque fantasy, complete with demons, a talking bat, and a mad monk whose body parts keep falling off. The scene where Rasputin invades Anastasia’s dream and tries to get her to jump to her death is a nice bit of Bluthian morbidity.

https://t.co/7hW2HGjw6Y

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Bluth’s final feature, the PG-rated sci-fi adventure Titan A.E. (2000), is often described as darker and edgier than his earlier work. I find it less disturbing than most of his films, maybe because I expect dark imagery in an action movie. It’s a lot more jarring in a film about adorable mice. Still, snapping a character’s neck onscreen is pretty intense for a PG movie.

https://t.co/m4L9fFmKQI

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Bluth brought the same taste for the macabre to the Dragon’s Lair arcade games, which feature some of his most imaginative character designs.

https://t.co/VjhnVZzWnJ

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Bluth’s storytelling can be haphazard, but I admire his commitment to full animation in the classic Disney style and his willingness to take his films in strange directions. There are plenty of pleasantly forgettable children’s movies, but a traumatic Don Bluth moment has a way of lodging itself deep in your subconscious. As Bluth himself once said, “If you don’t give the people something to really be frightened of, then when the salvation moment comes, it’s not as sweet.”

https://t.co/5nSoeo0g2K

— Cartoon Study (@CartoonStudy) November 20, 2026

Which scenes in Bluth’s movies got under your skin as a kid? Let us know in the comments. We’ll close with one last bit of nightmare fuel from An American Tail.

https://t.co/LsNH6fWXhy
